title: MIME Parameter Value and Encoded Word Extensions
summary: Extends the way MIME parameter values, such as filenames, are written so they can use other character sets and be split across several pieces. It also extends encoded words to name the language of the text. It replaces RFC 2184.

plainLanguage.summary: Email headers used to understand only plain English letters. This lets them carry names with accents or other alphabets and say what language they are in.

questions: how to encode non-ascii filenames in mime
what does title*0 mean in a mime header
how do mime parameter continuations work
subtitle: How MIME parameters such as filenames can carry non-ASCII text, a language tag, and be split across several pieces.

tldr.problem: MIME parameter values such as filenames are limited to 7-bit US-ASCII, can be damaged by header line folding when long, and cannot say what language they are in.
tldr.mechanism: Parameter names get an asterisk suffix: a numbered section (title*0, title*1) splits a long value, and a trailing asterisk marks a value written as charset'language'text with %XX percent-encoded octets. Encoded words also gain an optional language tag after an asterisk.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2184 and updates RFC 2045, RFC 2047 and RFC 2183, while the RFC itself warns these mechanisms should be reserved for real need.

today: RFC 2231 is a Proposed Standard from November 1997 and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It obsoletes RFC 2184 and updates RFC 2045, RFC 2047 and RFC 2183.

sections.title: Three Limits of MIME Parameters
sections.content:
MIME media types and dispositions can have parameters, such as the filename parameter of an attachment. They appear in the Content-Type and Content-Disposition header fields, which brings three limits.

  • Header lines are folded under RFC 822 rules, which makes long values problematic.
  • Headers are limited to 7-bit US-ASCII, and the encoded words of RFC 2047 are not available to parameter values.
  • Character set is not enough to display some text properly. Language is needed too, for example to read text aloud correctly.

The extensions are syntactically compatible with existing MIME implementations. The RFC adds an important note: the mechanisms are somewhat unwieldy in use, so they should be reserved for situations where a real need exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Email labels had three problems: only plain letters, trouble when too long, and no way to say which language they were in. This memo fixes all three.

sections.title: Parameter Value Continuations
sections.content:
Long values may be truncated or damaged by line wrapping. The fix must not change the syntax of the header lines and must not depend on parameter order, since MIME parameters are not order sensitive.

The solution is to use several parameters for one value. An asterisk followed by a decimal count marks the pieces. The count starts at 0 and goes up by 1, with no leading zeroes and no gaps. The original value is recovered by concatenating the sections in order.

Quotes around a value are part of the syntax, not of the value, and mixing quoted and unquoted sections is explicitly permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: If a sentence does not fit on one line, you write it on numbered cards: card 0, card 1, card 2. Put the cards in order and you have the sentence back.

sections.title: Character Set and Language in Values
sections.content:
A trailing asterisk on a parameter name (title*) signals that the value may begin with character set and language information. Single quotes separate the three parts: charset'language'value. A percent sign flags an octet written in hexadecimal, as in RFC 2047.

Either the charset or the language may be left empty, but both single quotes MUST still be present. Leaving a field empty MUST NOT be used to mean a default: parameter definitions MUST NOT assign a default character set or language.

The mechanisms can be combined with continuations. Language and character set appear only at the start of the whole value, so continuations cannot switch to another charset or language. A continued value may mix encoded and unencoded segments, but the first segment MUST be encoded if charset and language are given.
sections.plainLanguage: A label can start with a tag saying which alphabet and language it uses. Special characters are written as a percent sign and two letters or digits, a secret code that the reader turns back into the real character.

sections.title: Language in Encoded Words
sections.content:
RFC 2047 encoded words carry non-ASCII text in message headers, but only name a character set. This RFC adds an optional language by suffixing the charset with an asterisk and a language tag.

The ABNF changes to encoded-word := "=?" charset ["*" language] "?" encoded-text "?=". Such headers are mainly meant for display, which is why a language tag is useful.

If character sets later offer inline language labeling, those facilities SHOULD be used in preference to these, since they allow language switching in the middle of a string. All the mechanisms here allow language labels to be omitted to leave room for that.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag on an email sender can now also say which language the name is in, like a flag next to the name.

sections.title: Grammar Changes and IMAP
sections.content:
The ABNF of RFC 2045 is rewritten so that a parameter is either a regular-parameter or an extended-parameter. A parameter name may carry an optional section: *0 for the initial section and *1 to *9 followed by more digits for the others. The extended forms add the trailing asterisk. The ext-octet rule is a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits.

For IMAP4, servers SHOULD decode parameter value continuations when generating the BODY and BODYSTRUCTURE fetch attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The formal rulebook for what a label may look like was updated to allow the number cards and the alphabet tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not discuss security issues. It says it is not believed to raise any security issues beyond those already endemic in electronic mail and present in fully conforming implementations of MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors think this change adds no new dangers beyond what email already has.
